efbd60192a:
This chapter covers the Message Batches API from first principles, and the design decision around it: when work should run synchronously, streamed, or as a batch.

Here is what it walks through:

  • the request shape and custom_id;
  • the batch lifecycle and every field on the batch object;
  • the four result types, and which ones you pay for;
  • the limits and the 24-hour window;
  • polling, and resubmitting only what failed;
  • combining batches with prompt caching;
  • why a client-side tool loop cannot run inside one batch request;
  • a decision framework for realtime versus batch versus streaming;
  • how an SLA sets your submission cadence;
  • the Bedrock and Vertex equivalents.

Official sample question 1 of the CCDV-F guide (overnight, cost-sensitive work) is answered by this chapter.
3f08a581e0: Reading time: about 2 hours  ·  Companion code, 16 runnable examples: ccdvf-companion/07-batch-api/ (run bash run_all.sh). Every example runs offline against fake_batch.py, a simulated batch service with a hand-advanced clock, so a 24-hour batch completes in milliseconds.
804644ec2a: Neighbouring chapters: chapter 05 owns the shape of one Messages request, errors and rate limits. Chapter 06 owns streaming and the Bedrock/Vertex platforms in general. Chapter 15 covers cost modelling and cache mechanics in depth, and chapter 21 covers tool loops. This chapter owns asynchronous, bulk use of the same request, and the realtime-versus-batch decision.
10a303f80d:
The chapter rests on two sentences.

The Message Batches API takes up to 100,000 ordinary Messages requests at once, each tagged with your own custom_id, runs them asynchronously within 24 hours (usually under one), and charges 50% of the standard price for every request that succeeds.

You give up the latency guarantee and the conversation (no streaming, no client tool loop inside a request, results in any order), so batch is the right answer exactly when no person or process is waiting on an individual result and the job can tolerate the 24-hour worst case.
bc1a3d7804:
Everything else in the chapter follows from those two sentences.

  • Results arrive later and out of order. So you need a correlation key and a reconciliation step.
  • Individual requests can fail while the batch succeeds. So you need per-request outcome handling, and a way to resubmit only the failures.
  • The window is 24 hours, not one. So a deadline-driven job needs a submission time worked back from the worst case, or a fallback path.
  • A batch request is one call with nobody to answer it. So a model that asks for a client tool simply stops.
  • The discount applies to tokens. So it stacks with prompt caching, which turns a large shared prefix into the biggest saving available on the platform.
718904b1d4:
On the exam this objective shows up both directly and indirectly.

Directly: official sample question 1 describes overnight, cost-sensitive processing, and the answer is the Batch API. The distractors are streaming, more concurrency, a bigger model, or caching alone.

Indirectly: a question on cost (5.4), rate limits (chapter 05) or debugging (D4) often has a batch-shaped answer or a batch-shaped trap. Think of a team that put an interactive feature on batch, or reran a whole batch because 2% failed.

The stems are easy to spot: "nightly", "overnight", "backfill", "by tomorrow morning", "cost is the main concern", "no user is waiting". So are the traps: "the agent must look up each customer", "results are needed within 30 seconds", "the answers were attached to the wrong records".
e97de44f83: Batch processing is the oldest pattern in computing, and every generation has rediscovered why it exists. The lineage is worth knowing. The Batches API makes the same trade every earlier batch system made, and the design problems you will meet (correlation, partial failure, windows, reruns) are the ones those systems already solved.
b4af0de6eb:
On mainframes, interactive work ran during the day: CICS transactions at a bank teller's terminal. Batch work ran overnight, when the terminals were quiet: JCL job streams for posting, statement runs and billing. The machine was expensive and fixed in size. Filling the night with work nobody was waiting for made the same hardware do twice as much.

Every batch job had a schedule, an input dataset, an output dataset, a return code per step, and a restart procedure. The restart procedure mattered. A job that failed at 3 a.m. with half its records posted could not simply be rerun from the top without double-posting.

Telecom billing still works this way in many places. Rating and invoicing runs are batch jobs with checkpoints, and a "bill run" has a cut-off time worked back from the date invoices must be printed.
852ae90893:
Spring Batch (2008) formalised the same ideas for the JVM:

  • a Job made of Steps;
  • chunk-oriented processing (read, process, write N items per transaction);
  • a JobRepository that records every execution, so a restart resumes from the last committed chunk;
  • skip and retry policies per item;
  • job parameters that make each run identifiable, so the same run is never launched twice.

In parallel, message-oriented middleware (JMS, then Kafka) decoupled producers from consumers. You publish work with a correlation id, and someone processes it when they can.

If you have built either, you already know the shape of a good batch pipeline. The Batches API removes the worker side, because Anthropic runs it. It leaves you the submission, tracking and reconciliation side, which is where the bugs were anyway.
b20b6fde76:
Cloud providers offered batch modes for machine-learning inference well before large language models. You submitted a file of inputs to object storage and got a file of predictions back.

When LLM APIs arrived, providers met the old mainframe economics in a new form. GPU fleets are expensive and must be sized for the daytime peak of interactive traffic, so off-peak capacity sits idle. A batch endpoint with a relaxed completion window lets the provider schedule work into those troughs and pass part of the saving on.

OpenAI introduced a batch endpoint with a 24-hour window and a 50% discount in 2024. Anthropic introduced the Message Batches API later the same year, with the same headline terms (launched in beta in late 2024 and generally available shortly after; check the docs for exact dates). Amazon Bedrock and Google Vertex AI offer their own batch inference services for Claude models, built on their storage services (section 15).
51e3ed79ca:
Two things make LLM batch work different from a classic batch job.

First, the unit of work is not deterministic. Rerunning a request can produce a different answer. So "just rerun the batch" is not idempotent the way reposting a ledger with checks is: it can change answers you already stored and used.

Second, the unit of work can be conversational. The synchronous API supports multi-step tool use, and people expect batches to do the same. They cannot, for a structural reason covered in section 11.

Both differences turn into exam questions.
8a52d062b3:
Most batch questions are classic batch-engineering questions in LLM clothing:

  • "how do you match results to inputs" (correlation id);
  • "what do you do about the 3% that failed" (resubmit only those);
  • "when must you submit to meet a 7 a.m. deadline" (work back from the worst-case window);
  • "can the batch do X interactively" (no).

If an option would be wrong for a Spring Batch job, it is almost always wrong here too.
b1cc92ebb8:
A synchronous request reserves capacity the moment you send it. The provider has to schedule your prompt on an accelerator immediately, keep the connection open, and return within seconds. To keep that promise to every customer at once, it must provision for the peak of combined demand, plus headroom.

Demand is not flat. It follows working hours across time zones, with bursts when products launch and troughs at night and at weekends. Whatever capacity sits idle in the troughs has already been paid for.
849d36e7f5:
A batch request carries a different promise: the answer within a window, up to 24 hours. That lets the scheduler treat batch work as filler. It can run your requests when interactive load is low, pack them densely, and pause them when a burst arrives.

Serving a token in a trough costs much less than serving it at the peak. The discount is the provider sharing that difference. Anthropic's terms at the time of writing: all batch usage is charged at 50% of standard prices, input and output, for every active model (verified against the batch processing documentation, October 2026).
bcb8022812:
Three consequences follow, and each one shows up in design questions.

First, completion time is not a constant. Most batches finish within an hour, but processing slows when demand is high. On a busy day, requests can sit unstarted until the window closes and come back as expired. The documented guarantee is the window, not the typical time.

Second, batch work is off your interactive rate limits. It has its own limits, on Batches API calls and on the number of requests waiting to be processed. So moving a nightly fan-out to batch also stops it eating the requests-per-minute budget your daytime product depends on.

Third, the model, prompt format and output quality are identical. Batch is not a cheaper, weaker model. It is the same model on a different delivery contract. An option that says "batch reduces quality" is wrong.
d2c35ec1ee:
A batch is a list of entries, and each entry has exactly two fields. custom_id is your correlation key. params is the body you would send to POST /v1/messages: model, max_tokens, system, messages, tools, tool_choice, thinking settings, output_config and so on.

There is no batch-specific prompt format and no batch-specific model. Entries in one batch can use different models and different prompts. A single batch can mix a Haiku classification with a Sonnet summarisation.
1454726511:
custom_id has precise rules. It must be 1 to 64 characters long. It may contain only letters, digits, hyphens and underscores (^[a-zA-Z0-9_-]{1,64}$). And it must be unique within the batch.

Business keys often break the first rule. An order number like ORD/2026/10/09#A17 contains slashes and a hash. Don't try to put JSON or several fields into the id. Encode the key into the allowed alphabet and keep a lookup table (or use a surrogate key from your own database), as 01_batch_shape.py does.

Some mistakes fail the whole create call, because they are checked when the batch is submitted: a violation of the id rules, a duplicate id, an empty list, or more than 100,000 entries. Problems inside params are different. Each request is validated when it is processed, so one malformed body becomes one errored result and leaves its neighbours alone.
f4ce7fedfb:
The types in the example are the ones the Python SDK documents. They are typed dictionaries, so plain dicts work too. The typed form catches a misspelt field at your desk, instead of at 2 a.m. when the result says errored.

Everything the synchronous API supports in a request body is supported here, with three documented exceptions: stream: true (results come back as a file, not a stream), the speed parameter for fast mode, and max_tokens: 0. Each of those is a validation error for that request.

Vision, documents, system prompts, multi-turn message histories, extended thinking, tool definitions, server tools such as web search and code execution, and most beta features all work (verified against the batch processing documentation, October 2026).
242ae4c361:
A batch hides a prompt bug for as long as the batch takes. If the output format is wrong, you learn it when 50,000 results arrive: all wrong, all paid for.

So test first. Run 10 to 50 representative items through the synchronous API with the identical params. Check the outputs with the same validator the pipeline uses. Fix the prompt, then submit.

Example 14_validate_on_sample_first.py shows the loop: 0% valid with the first system prompt, 100% with the second, then the batch. The CCAR-F guide states the same rule as "refine the prompt on a sample before batch-processing large volumes".
b0960911dd: The create call returns immediately with a batch object. Nothing has been processed yet; you have a ticket. From then on the batch moves through at most three processing states, and you observe it by retrieving the object again. The states are deliberately few, because the interesting detail lives per request, not per batch.
7acf869354:
in_progress is the initial state. canceling is set immediately after a cancel request. ended is set once every request in the batch has a final result and the results are ready.

There is no failed state for a batch. A batch in which every single request errored still ends normally, with request_counts.errored equal to the total. That is the first thing a monitoring dashboard gets wrong. Alerting on "batch ended" tells you nothing. Alerting on the ratio of succeeded to total does.
0319421d88: The companion example 02_lifecycle.py submits 5,000 requests to the simulated service and polls every 30 simulated seconds. The trace shows what a real dashboard sees. processing falls, succeeded rises, and the status flips to ended in one step when the last request finishes.
a97cd97f6e:
Besides create and retrieve, the API has four more operations:

  • List returns the workspace's batches, newest first, with pagination (the SDK auto-paginates).
  • Cancel stops a batch that is still processing.
  • Results streams the JSONL output of an ended batch.
  • Delete removes an ended batch and its data. An in-progress batch must be cancelled first.

Batches are scoped to a workspace. Requests from that workspace can see them, and so can Console users with permission to view the workspace's batches. Nobody else can.

This catches teams that separate environments by workspace. A batch submitted with the staging key will not be visible to the production job that polls for it. That is a common "batch not found" ticket.
0828ffae22:
When the batch ends, its results are a JSON Lines file: one JSON object per line, one line per request. Each line carries the custom_id and a result object whose type is succeeded, errored, canceled or expired.

A succeeded result contains the complete Message object, exactly as the synchronous API would have returned it, including content, stop_reason and usage. An errored result contains an error in the standard API error shape.

The documentation recommends streaming the results rather than downloading the whole file into memory. The SDK's results() iterator does exactly that. It matters when 100,000 summaries add up to hundreds of megabytes.
d08e18efac:
The documentation is explicit: results can come back in any order and may not match the order of the requests. This is not an edge case to handle someday. It is the normal behaviour of a system that runs requests in parallel on many machines and writes results as they finish. The only correct join is on custom_id.

Example 03_results_by_custom_id.py shows the bug. Zipping the submitted list with the results list attached 19 of 20 summaries to the wrong ticket. Nothing raises an exception. The summaries are well formed, plausible and wrong, and in a ticketing system they would be written to customer records.

In the Spring Batch analogy, this is processing a reply queue without reading the correlation id header.
dc69162990: The reconciliation assertion is cheap insurance. It catches two problems before any data is written. One is a request that never comes back (it should not happen, but a pipeline bug that drops entries before submission can make it look that way). The other is an id you did not submit, such as a result file from the wrong batch.
3969d4fb95:
succeeded means the model produced a message. It does not mean the message is what you wanted. Every rule from chapter 05 still applies:

  • check stop_reason, because a max_tokens result is a truncated answer and a refusal is a 200-equivalent that is not success;
  • validate structured output against its schema;
  • read content blocks by type, not by position.

A batch makes these checks more important, not less, because nobody is reading the outputs as they arrive.
b8ba80c8ff:
errored means no message was created. The documentation names two causes, invalid requests and internal server errors, and they need different handling. The error type tells you which one you have.

An invalid_request_error means the body was wrong: a missing max_tokens, stream: true, an unknown field, a malformed content block. Resending it unchanged fails again. It needs a code or data fix first.

A server-side error such as api_error or overloaded_error is transient, and can be resent as-is. This is chapter 05's retry-versus-fix classification of status codes, applied per request.
b5c284fab6:
expired means the 24-hour window closed before the request was sent to the model. The request was fine; the day was busy. Resend it, in a new batch, or synchronously if a deadline is close.

canceled means you (or an operator) cancelled the batch before this request was sent to the model. Whether to resend depends on why you cancelled. If it was to fix a prompt bug, the cancelled requests should go out with the fixed prompt. If the job was abandoned, nothing goes out.
0767ef0c66:
Only succeeded results are billed. Errored, canceled and expired requests cost nothing (verified against the batch processing documentation, October 2026).

This has a practical consequence for cancelling. A batch you cancel because of a bug costs you only the requests that already ran. It also means a batch with a high error rate is cheap but useless. That is why the success ratio, not the bill, is the health metric.

One more cost detail. Batches may go slightly over a workspace's configured spend limit, because many requests are in flight when the limit is reached. If a hard budget matters, leave headroom.
74b5f846f9: Example 04_result_types.py runs that handler against a simulated busy day. It sends 200 requests, two of them deliberately invalid bodies (max_tokens: 0 and stream: true). It adds a 5% server-error rate, and gives the window only enough capacity for about half the work.
e9d937a49d:
Notice two things in the trace.

First, the batch ended normally even though nearly half of it did not produce an answer. ended means "final", not "successful".

Second, the two invalid requests did not stop the batch or affect any other request. The documentation states that the failure of one request does not affect the processing of others. That isolation is why per-request validation is the right design, and why your pipeline must look at every line.
0c326372cd: The limits are few, and each one has a design consequence. All values below were checked against the batch processing documentation in October 2026. Rate-limit numbers live on the separate rate limits page and vary by usage tier, so check the docs for your organisation's values.
9f40fabed6:
The count and size limits interact. Short classification prompts hit 100,000 requests at a few tens of megabytes. Contract review with 40-page documents inline hits 256 MB at a few thousand requests.

So a chunker must check both. It should measure the serialised size of each entry rather than guess, and leave a little headroom. If a single entry is larger than the limit on its own, no amount of chunking helps. That document needs the Files API (chapter 06) or a different design.

Example 09_chunking_limits.py splits 250,000 short requests into 100,000 + 100,000 + 50,000. It splits a set of large requests into many small batches when the byte limit binds.
80943bb7d9:
The 24-hour window is the limit people misread.

It is not "the batch takes 24 hours"; most finish in under an hour. It is not "requests time out after 24 hours of running"; a request that started is allowed to finish. It is the deadline by which a request must have been sent to the model.

A request still waiting when the window closes is marked expired. The batch ends, and the expired requests cost nothing. So on a busy day a large batch can end with a mix of succeeded and expired results, and your pipeline has to resubmit the expired ones. The consequence for deadlines is in section 13.
631e90fed3:
The 29-day retention is measured from creation. After that you can still see the batch object, but the results can no longer be downloaded.

Treat the Batches API as a delivery mechanism, not a store. Stream the results into your own database or object store when the batch ends. Keep your own record of which batch produced which row.

Batch processing stores request and response data for up to 29 days. If you have data-handling obligations (customer data in telecom is usually covered by them), delete the batch once you have its results. That removes this copy early.
1f04e6c2fe:
The API is pull-based: you find out a batch has ended by asking. The documented pattern is a loop that retrieves the batch, checks processing_status, and sleeps.

The question is how long to sleep. Too short, and you burn requests against the Batches API rate limit and clutter your own logs. The information does not change faster because you asked more often. Too long, and you add latency to a job that has a deadline.

The usual answer is a growing interval with a cap, plus a deadline after which you stop waiting and act.
0718433698:
Example 10_poll_backoff.py compares this with a one-second loop on the simulated service. For a batch that took 30 minutes, the tight loop made 1,804 retrieve calls. The backoff loop made 8, and noticed the end six minutes later.

Six minutes of detection latency on a job measured in hours is a good trade. If the six minutes matter, cap the interval lower: two minutes gives at most two minutes of lag, at a few dozen calls an hour. Don't drop below a minute without a reason. The documented example polls every 60 seconds.
a6a5d55b04:
In a Spring application, the natural home for this is not a thread that sleeps. Use a scheduled method (@Scheduled(fixedDelay = 120_000)). It loads every open batch id from your job table, retrieves each one, and advances the ones that ended.

That design survives restarts and scales to many concurrent jobs. It also makes the job table the single source of truth, which section 14 relies on.

On Bedrock, job state changes can be delivered through Amazon EventBridge instead of polling. On the Claude API, polling is the documented mechanism (check the docs for any notification feature added since).
609f4e1bb1:
Every large batch has some failures: a few server errors, perhaps some expired requests on a busy day, perhaps a handful of invalid bodies from bad input data. The tempting response is to rerun the whole batch. It is wrong for three reasons.

  • It pays again for every request that already succeeded. A 5% failure rate then costs 100% more instead of 5% more.
  • It produces new answers for records you may already have stored and acted on. Generation is not deterministic, so those answers can differ, and now you have two versions of the truth.
  • It does nothing about invalid requests, which fail again identically.
c50419def1:
The right design is a ledger: a record per custom_id with its status and attempt count. Each round, select the entries that still need work, build a new batch from just those, and update the ledger from the results.

Each kind of failure has its own route. Server errors and expired entries go back as-is. Invalid entries go to a repair step (fix the data or the code) or to a person. Entries that fail repeatedly go to a dead-letter list after a capped number of attempts, the same as any message consumer.

custom_ids only need to be unique within one batch. So you can reuse the same id when you resubmit, which keeps the ledger keyed on your business identity.
ac2b49d9b9:
Example 05_resubmit_failed_only.py runs both strategies against 1,000 documents with a 5% transient failure rate on the first attempt. Rerunning everything took two full runs and cost $0.0014 in the simulation. The ledger took one full round plus a 50-request round and cost $0.0007, about half.

At production scale the ratio is the same. And the second benefit, that stored answers are never regenerated, matters more than the money.
be652334a8:
In Spring Batch terms, the ledger is the JobRepository plus a skip policy, and the dead-letter list is the skip listener's output.

If you already run Spring Batch, a clean implementation has two jobs. The first has a reader that selects pending and retry rows from the ledger table, and a writer that submits one batch per chunk and records the batch id. The second is a scheduled job that collects ended batches and updates ledger rows. The database transaction around "record batch id" is what makes the pipeline restartable.
5a2d14587c:
The two biggest cost levers on the platform stack.

Prompt caching (chapter 15) makes a repeated prefix cheaper to read. A cache read costs a tenth of the base input price. Writing to the cache costs 1.25 times the base price for the 5-minute lifetime, or twice the base price for the 1-hour lifetime. The batch discount then halves the result.

The textbook case is a job that sends the same 6,000-token policy manual with each of 2,000 contract checks. Without caching, it pays for 12 million input tokens of manual. With caching, it pays one write plus many cheap reads, and the batch halves all of it.
281f06e872:
There is a catch specific to batches, and the documentation states it plainly. Batch requests are processed concurrently and in no particular order, so cache hits are provided on a best-effort basis. Typical hit rates range from 30% to 98%, depending on traffic patterns.

The reason is simple. Two requests with the same prefix that start at the same moment on different machines cannot both read a cache entry that neither has written yet.

The documentation gives three ways to improve hit rates:

  • include identical cache_control blocks in every request;
  • keep a steady stream of requests, so entries do not expire;
  • share as much cached content as possible.

It also recommends the 1-hour cache duration for batches with shared context, because a batch can take longer than five minutes to work through.
7351c13bc5: The variable part (the contract) goes after the cached block. Nothing that varies per request may appear before or inside it. A timestamp or a customer name in the system prompt silently breaks every hit. The rules on what invalidates a cache are in chapter 15. In a batch they bite harder, because you won't notice for an hour.
d29c94665b:
The honest way to know whether caching paid off is to read usage on the results: cache_read_input_tokens versus cache_creation_input_tokens.

Example 07_batch_plus_caching.py simulates the 2,000-contract job at three hit rates. The simulation is pessimistic by design: every miss is charged as a cache write at the 1-hour price. That makes the lesson visible:
97aa13e415:
Three practical rules follow.

First, put enough shared content in the prefix to make caching worthwhile, and keep it byte-identical across entries (same tools, same system blocks, same order).

Second, sort or group requests so those sharing a prefix are submitted together. Mixing ten different prefixes in one batch spreads the hits thin.

Third, if a job has a large shared prefix and you need predictable hit rates, consider a warm-up. Send one synchronous request with the prefix to write the cache, then submit the batch while the entry is live. Whether this helps depends on how quickly the batch starts, which you do not control. So measure it (and check the docs for current guidance).

The full cache-pricing arithmetic is in chapter 15, including the minimum cacheable prefix length per model and the break-even number of reads.
ede8a5802e: A synchronous agent works by repetition. You send a request with tool definitions. The model replies with stop_reason: "tool_use" and a tool_use block. Your code runs the tool and sends a new request containing the assistant turn and a tool_result. And so on, until end_turn. Each step is a separate API call, and the loop lives in your code (chapters 01 and 21).
9d5ef79bdb:
A batch entry is one API call. When it is processed, the model produces one assistant turn and the request is finished.

If that turn ends in tool_use, the result is a succeeded message with stop_reason: "tool_use", and a tool call that nobody will answer. There is no hook for your code to run in the middle of a batch request.

That is what "no multi-turn tool calling within one batch request" means. It is structural, not a missing feature. The whole point of the batch is that the provider runs the work without you.
778299af9b:
The documentation lists "multi-turn conversations" and "tool use" as supported, which confuses people. Both statements are true at the request level.

A batch entry may contain a long messages history, including earlier tool_use and tool_result turns. So you can batch the next step of many conversations.

Tool definitions are allowed, so the model can choose to call a tool. Forced tool use is a common way to get structured output from a batch: the tool's input is the answer, and you never run anything.

Server tools (web search, web fetch, code execution) run inside Anthropic's infrastructure, so their loop happens without you. In batches they get more iterations per turn before returning pause_turn. A paused result is unfinished. You continue it by submitting the paused assistant content in a follow-up request.

What a batch cannot do is wait for your code to execute a client tool and continue.
120b53d9ce: Pre-fetch the data (the usual answer). Say the model needs a customer's plan to write a recommendation. Look the plan up yourself before building the batch, and put it in the prompt. The tool was only ever a way of getting data into context, and in a batch you know in advance which data each item needs. Example 08_no_tool_loop.py shows the broken version (every result ends in tool_use) and this fix (every result ends in end_turn in one batch).
d1fcc0d5ba: Run tool rounds between batches. Sometimes the data genuinely depends on the model's first step, because it decides which of several lookups to make. Then collect the tool_use blocks from batch 1 and run the tools. Submit batch 2, whose entries carry the original user turn, the assistant turn from batch 1, and the tool_result. Each round can take up to 24 hours. So this works only for jobs with a multi-day tolerance and a small, bounded number of rounds. The same example shows it.
c62948b539: Use the synchronous API with asynchronous workers. If the work is a real agent with an open-ended number of steps, it does not belong in a batch. Run it at full price on a worker pool (a queue, a thread pool or Spring's @Async) with client-side rate control. This is still "background" processing. It just isn't the Batches API.
502d58af6c:
Picture a scenario that says "the agent must call our inventory API for each item", then offers the Batch API for cost reasons. It is testing this section. If the lookups can be done up front, batch with pre-fetched context is the best answer. If the agent decides at each step what to do next, the Batches API is the wrong tool regardless of cost.

The CCAR-F guide phrases the rule as "no multi-turn tool calling inside one batch request". The CCDV-F objective expects the same understanding.
0f31664b78: The decision looks like a cost question, and that is exactly why people get it wrong. Cost is the last question, not the first. Start with the constraints that rule options out, then let cost choose among what remains. There are four questions, in order.
f54c9e6b1b: Is a person or a blocking process waiting on this individual result? Examples: a chat reply, an IDE suggestion, a pre-merge review that gates a developer, a fraud check before payment, an agent step inside a live conversation. If yes, the answer is synchronous. Batch is out regardless of price, because "usually under an hour" is not a response time.
f458d6920b: Can the whole job tolerate the 24-hour worst case? That means the documented window, not the typical hour. "By tomorrow evening" can. "By 7 a.m., data lands at 1 a.m." cannot be guaranteed by batch alone; section 13 shows how to make it work with a fallback. "Within five minutes of upload" cannot.
0dccd6a4d0: Among what remains, which is cheapest and simplest to operate? For bulk work that passed the first three questions, batch is 50% cheaper and takes the load off your interactive rate limits. For synchronous work, streaming is a presentation choice. Use it when a person watches a long output appear (chapter 06), not for machine-to-machine calls.
206775178e:
The table is the heart of the exam objective. Notice the two patterns that trap people.

A job can be "background" without being batch-suitable. An agentic weekly report is background, but an open-ended tool loop rules out the Batches API.

And a job can be cost-sensitive without being batch-suitable. A fraud check is high-volume and cost matters, but a process is waiting.

Example 12_decision_framework.py encodes the four questions as a function, with these cases as tests.
63a5d02f99:
Hybrids are normal. One product can use streaming for its chat, synchronous calls for its tool-using agent, and batch for its nightly re-indexing and its evaluation suite. All of it runs against the same model and prompt library.

The CCAR-F guide's official sample makes this point for CI. The pre-merge check stays synchronous, because a developer is blocked on it. The overnight technical-debt report moves to batch. The architecture question is not "which API do we use" but "which API does each workload use".
7732a8c3b0:
Streaming does not make a request cheaper, or the model faster in total. It delivers the same tokens as they are produced, so time to first token drops to roughly the prefill time (chapter 06). It matters when a person watches a long output.

For a backend service that parses a JSON answer, streaming adds complexity for no benefit. And it isn't available in batches at all: stream: true in a batch entry is a validation error.

An option that offers streaming as the fix for a cost problem, or batch as the fix for perceived latency, has the two confused.
4ef9ee0f7b:
A batch job with a deadline needs a schedule worked back from that deadline. The arithmetic must use the documented window, not the typical completion time.

Say results must be ready by 07:00 and you submit at 01:00. On a typical day you meet the deadline, finishing by about 02:00. On a slow one you miss it, because requests can stay unstarted until 01:00 the next day. Whether that is acceptable is a business decision, but it must be an explicit one.
7166c2d988: Submit earlier or more often. If the deadline is 24 hours or more after the data is ready, a single submission is guaranteed to finish in time. If data arrives continuously (orders, tickets, call records), submit smaller batches through the day, for example hourly, instead of one large batch at night. Each batch then carries less risk, results flow sooner, and a slow batch affects only one hour of data. This is what "submission frequency from the SLA" means in the CCAR-F task statement: you choose the cadence so that the window plus processing fits inside the SLA.
af33a70046: Add a fallback cut-off. Pick a time before the deadline: the deadline minus the time the realtime path needs to finish the leftovers. At that time, if the batch has not ended, cancel it, collect the partial results, and process the remainder synchronously at full price. You pay full price only for the slow-day remainder. On typical days the fallback never fires.
4814e843aa:
Example 11_sla_cadence.py simulates a slow day. It submits 12,000 account summaries at 01:00, with capacity for only about 7,200 of them before the 05:30 cut-off.

At the cut-off the batch is still in_progress. The job cancels it, collects the 7,200 succeeded results, and sends the 4,800 remaining synchronously. Everything is done before 07:00. On its worst day the job paid batch price for 60% of the work; on a typical day it pays batch price for all of it.

In Java you would implement the cut-off as a second @Scheduled trigger (cron 0 30 5 * * *) that checks the job table. The fallback is a bounded executor that drains the leftovers through the synchronous client, with the same retry policy as chapter 05.
fb38796e8a: Size the fallback path for the worst case you are willing to absorb, including its rate limits. 4,800 synchronous calls in 90 minutes is about 53 per minute. That must fit inside the organisation's requests-per-minute and token limits, alongside daytime traffic that may be starting. If it doesn't fit, move the cut-off earlier.
21893046f8: Put sections 04 to 13 together, and a production pipeline has six stages. None of them is complicated. The failures in practice come from skipping one.
70e18017df: Select. Choose the inputs and give the run an identity, for example ticket-tagging/2026-10-09. The identity is how a rerun knows it is a rerun.
aec235fc08: Validate on a sample. Run a few dozen representative items synchronously with the exact params, and validate the outputs (example 14). You can skip this once a prompt is stable and covered by an evaluation suite. Never skip it for a new or changed prompt.
2a446003af: Submit and persist. Write the batch id to the ledger immediately after create returns, keyed by job identity and chunk number. Example 15_idempotent_submission.py shows the failure this prevents. A worker crashes after creating a batch, the scheduler reruns the job, and a second identical batch is created and paid for. With the ledger, the rerun finds the id and resumes polling. A small gap remains: a crash between create returning and the ledger write. Close it on restart by listing recent batches and matching on request count and creation time.
b24253eb71: Collect and route. Stream results, join on custom_id, and reconcile in both directions. Route each result by type and stop_reason, and validate structured output. Write successes to your store, update the ledger, and feed retry rows into the next round. Then emit metrics: success ratio, expired count, cost from summed usage, batch duration, cache hit ratio.
85dafff11e:
Two operational habits round this out.

Alert on ratios, not on events. "Batch ended" is not news. "Succeeded below 98%" or "expired above zero" is.

And keep the model ID pinned in the job's configuration (chapter 10). Then a model change is a deliberate, evaluated change to the job, not something that happens to it between Tuesday's and Wednesday's runs.
595d42f384:
The Message Batches API is a Claude API (first-party) feature. Chapter 06's portability map already notes that it is not available through the Bedrock or Vertex Messages endpoints. Each cloud has its own batch service instead, built on its storage and job infrastructure.

Exam questions on this are brief. Know that the equivalents exist, that they are separate services with their own request formats, and that the design rules of this chapter carry over.
2bd3494a93:
The Bedrock row is partly verified against the Bedrock user guide (October 2026). Bedrock batch inference:

  • reads input files from S3, in either the InvokeModel or Converse format;
  • writes output files to S3;
  • can publish job state changes to EventBridge;
  • is not supported for provisioned models;
  • processes each record independently, without multi-turn interaction or tool calling.

Details such as job timeouts, minimum record counts and the exact discount are on linked pages and change, so check the docs. For Vertex, check the docs for every detail beyond the existence of the service.

The point for an architect is that the pipeline of section 14 is the same on all three: validate, build with correlation keys, submit, persist the job id, poll, join, resubmit failures. Only the transport changes, from an API call to files in a bucket.
bd617cba83: Each of these has a broken-versus-fixed example in the companion folder. Most are classic batch-engineering mistakes. A few are specific to LLMs.
516406c88c:
Batch code is awkward to test against the real service. A full run can take an hour, failures are rare and not reproducible on demand, and every test costs money.

The companion's fake_batch.py takes the approach of the earlier chapters' fake clients one step further. It implements the batch surface (create, retrieve, list, cancel, results, delete) with the documented rules: custom_id validation at create time, per-request validation at processing time, shuffled result order, the four result types, billing only for successes, cancel semantics, 24-hour expiry and 29-day retention.

Time is a Clock you advance by hand. The poller receives clock.sleep instead of time.sleep, so a 24-hour scenario runs in milliseconds. Failure injection is a function of custom_id and attempt number. "5% fail once, then succeed" is one line, and a busy day is a capacity_s parameter.
72bbe1b906:
The suite in 16_test_suite.py covers the properties that matter: results unavailable before the end, every custom_id back exactly once, invalid requests isolated, stream: true rejected per request, duplicate ids rejecting the whole batch, the id pattern, the 50% price, the poller stopping at the end, and expiry.

In a Spring project the same idea is an interface over the batch client, with an in-memory implementation and a Clock bean. Spring already encourages injecting java.time.Clock. Then @Scheduled collectors and cut-off logic can be tested with a fixed clock.

As in chapter 05, be clear about what these tests prove: that your pipeline handles every outcome the service can produce. They prove nothing about the quality of the answers. That needs an evaluation run, and evaluation runs are themselves a good batch workload.
569c9a4f35: Before trusting the fake, run one small real batch (ten requests, one deliberately invalid) and compare its result shapes with what the fake produces. Example 01_batch_shape.py shows the request shapes. If the real service ever disagrees with the fake, the real service wins, and the fake should change.
1960f1c98f:
This is the official sample Q1 pattern: offline, latency-tolerant, cost-sensitive, with 20 hours of slack. The 24-hour window is acceptable once you note that 20 hours is slightly less than 24; a cut-off fallback, or an earlier submission, closes the gap. The batch discount halves the price and stacks with caching on the shared style guide. 300,000 items need three batches.

A buys latency nobody needs, and streaming does nothing for a machine consumer. C ignores the cost constraint without evidence that a larger model is needed. D is half the answer: caching helps, but it does not replace the 50% batch discount.
0e54b606d3:
Each request is processed independently, so there is no shared context to mix up (A). The documentation states that results may come back in any order and that custom_id is the key. Positional joining attaches correct summaries to the wrong records, with no error.

C does not match the symptom (all succeeded). D asks the model to carry a correlation id you already have. It might work, but it moves a deterministic join into a probabilistic output.
2bc5407e36:
Server errors and expired requests are transient: the same body will usually succeed. Invalid requests fail identically until the body changes, so C wastes a round on 60 guaranteed failures.

A pays again for 77,400 successes, and regenerates answers already in review, which may now differ. D silently loses 3% of contracts, which an extraction pipeline cannot do.

Errored and expired requests were not billed, so the targeted resubmission costs only the 2,600 requests.
d2945cba1f:
A batch request is a single turn. A client tool call ends it with stop_reason: "tool_use", and nobody returns the result. The data needed per customer is known in advance, so pre-fetching it turns the agent into a single-shot prompt that batches well.

A gets an answer without the data it needs. C misreads the stop reason. D is invalid: streaming is not supported in batches, and it would not create a return channel anyway. If the lookups were open-ended and model-driven, the right answer would be synchronous workers instead.
0148cde952:
The typical completion time is not the contract; the window is. Six hours of slack is a typical-day promise, so a deadline-driven job needs a fallback or an earlier cadence.

A is false: same model, same output. C is false: the limit is 100,000 requests (or 256 MB). D confuses the 24-hour processing window with the 29-day results retention.
d21e5cac7a: In 07_batch_plus_caching.py, find the hit rate at which caching breaks even against no caching for the 1-hour TTL. Then change the TTL to 5 minutes (write premium 1.25x) and find it again. Which TTL would you choose for a batch that takes 45 minutes? Why?
bbb0229e93: Done when: you can recite the lifecycle states, the four result types and which are billed, and the limits (100,000 requests, 256 MB, 24 hours, 29 days). You can name the three things a batch request cannot do (stream, fast mode, client tool loop). And you can classify any workload as realtime, streaming or batch in four questions.
